{{Short description|American mathematician (1939–2003)}}
'''Joaquín Bustoz Jr.''' (1939–2003) was an American mathematician who worked as a professor of mathematics at [[Arizona State University]]. His mathematical research concerned [[classical analysis]], including [[Fourier analysis]], [[summability methods]], [[univalent function]], [[orthogonal polynomials]] and  [[special functions]]. He made contributions to all of these topics, most notably in collaboration with [[Mourad Ismail]], Sergei Suslov and with his PhD students Luís Daniel Abreu, José Luis Cardoso and Luis Gordillo. But he was primarily known as a mentor to underrepresented minorities in mathematics.<ref name="maa"/>

Bustoz was born in [[Tempe, Arizona]]; his parents worked on the local farms and also for the [[Tempe Elementary School District]], which eventually named the Joaquin and Ramona Bustoz Elementary School after them. He graduated from Arizona State University in 1962 with a degree in mathematics, and after two years in California working for [[Univac]] returned to ASU,<ref name="maa">{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304053837/http://www.maa.org/programs/underrepresented-groups/summa/summa-archival-record/joaquin-bustoz|archive-date=March 4, 2016|url-status=dead|title=Joaquin Bustoz Jr.|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/underrepresented-groups/summa/summa-archival-record/joaquin-bustoz|work=Strengthening Underrepresented Minority Mathematics Achievement|publisher=[[Mathematical Association of America]]|accessdate=2015-08-03}}</ref> where he completed a doctorate in 1967 under the supervision of Walter Tandy Scott.<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=17278}}</ref> After teaching at the [[University of Cincinnati]] from 1969 to 1976, during which he also spent a year at the [[National University of Colombia]] as a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright Scholar]], he returned to ASU again as an associate professor in 1976, and was promoted to full professor in 1978.<ref name="maa"/><ref name="m4w"/> He chaired the ASU mathematics department from 1982 to 1985.<ref name="m4w"/>

In 1985, Bustoz founded the Summer Math–Science Honors program for high school students,<ref name="maa"/><ref name="obit">{{citation|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/azcentral/obituary.aspx?n=joaquin-bustoz&pid=1330487&|title=Joaquin Bustoz Obituary|newspaper=[[The Arizona Republic]]|date=August 20, 2003|accessdate=2015-08-03}}.</ref><ref name="m4w">{{citation|url=http://latinopm.com/education/it%E2%80%99s-a-math-math-math-math-world-4400|title=It's a math, math, math, math world; and 25 years later, ASU's Math–Science Honors Program is still prepping students for it|journal=Latino Perspectives|department=Education|date=November 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160528232501/http://latinopm.com/education/it%E2%80%99s-a-math-math-math-math-world-4400|archive-date=2016-05-28|url-status=dead}}</ref> which continues at ASU as the Joaquin Bustoz Math–Science Honors Program.<ref name="m4w"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://jbmshp.asu.edu/|title=Joaquin Bustoz Math-Science Honors Program|accessdate=2015-08-03}}.</ref> Bustoz also worked on mathematics education on the [[Navajo Nation]] and the [[Pima people|Pima reservations]].<ref name="maa"/> For his efforts, president [[Bill Clinton]] honored him in 1996 with the Presidential Award for Excellence in Science, Mathematics and Engineering Mentoring.<ref>{{citation|url=http://math.nist.gov/opsf/personal/bustoz.html|title=Joaquin Bustoz receives Presidential Mentoring Award|publisher=OP-SF Net|date=January 15, 1997|accessdate=2015-08-03}}.</ref>

He was killed by a car accident on August 13, 2003.<ref name="obit"/><ref name="m4w"/> As well as the Math–Science Honors program, the Joaquin Bustoz Jr. Professorship at ASU, held by [[Carlos Castillo-Chavez]], is named after Bustoz.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.asu.edu/news/faculty_students/castillo-chavez120103.htm|title=High profile mathematical epidemiologist equally serious about mentoring|journal=ASU News|date=December 1, 2003|first=James|last=Hathaway}}.</ref>
